one_liner: A wide-moat business worth owning, but it trades at 1.5x fair value. Interesting below about $215.

profile.what: S&P Global owns one of the two dominant credit-rating agencies, the S&P Dow Jones indices, and large financial and commodity data businesses built up through its merger with IHS Markit.
profile.money: Borrowers pay for ratings when they issue debt; fund managers pay licence fees linked to assets tracking its indices; banks and companies subscribe to its data. Ratings revenue rises and falls with bond issuance; the rest is largely recurring.
profile.valued: S&P Global is valued on P/E and free cash flow as a high-quality compounder. The multiple moves with debt-issuance volumes and interest-rate expectations.

summary.sentence: A ratings and index toll-keeper on the world's debt and fund markets.
strengths: Operating cash flow well above net income.
Capital-light: capex is a tiny share of cash flow.
risks: Ratings revenue falls when bond issuance slows.
Large goodwill from the IHS Markit merger.
Return on invested capital is moderate for the price.

meaning.what_it_does: Rates corporate and government debt, owns the S&P 500 and other indices, and sells financial and commodity data.
meaning.how_it_makes_money: Fees for credit ratings, index licensing fees tied to fund assets, and data subscriptions.
meaning.how_it_keeps_making_money: Borrowers need a rating from one of two dominant agencies; funds must license its indices.
meaning.how_it_could_stop: A long freeze in bond issuance, or regulation that weakens the rating agencies' position.

moat.summary: A rating from S&P or Moody's is the accepted standard for debt markets, and the S&P 500 is the world's most followed index.

industry.summary: Credit ratings and indices have been run the same way for decades.

management.summary: Returns nearly all free cash flow through buybacks and dividends; the IHS Markit merger added scale and goodwill.

valuation.method: Fair value is the average of two methods: (1) Owner cash flow: $5.3B a year: free cash flow less stock-based pay (median of the last three fiscal years and TTM). (2) Damodaran: cash flow to the firm: Sales grow 5–11% for five years, fading to 3%; operating margin held at 44%; cost of capital 8.6%. Cash added, debt subtracted. The owner cash flow method grows the cash for five years, then at half that rate, 3% after year ten, discounted at 10%. Stock-based pay is deducted because it is a real cost to owners.
